generatedProse.concept-context: Students across the School of Sport meet reflective models often, especially coaches and teachers on practicals and placements, where you reflect on how a session went. A simple three-stage model gives that reflection a shape: describe what happened in the session, reflect on why it went that way, and decide what to change. A sport scientist can apply the same three stages to a testing session, and a therapist to a treatment. It keeps a coaching logbook or reflective commentary from becoming a mere diary of events.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students use the three-stage model to reflect on the same training session that did not go well.

Tom writes: 'My session on passing drills was rushed and we ran over. It was stressful. I hope the next one goes better.' This describes the experience and names a feeling, but it stops there. It offers no real reflection on why it was rushed, and the 'hope' is not an action. Two of the three stages are missing.

Amara works through all three. Describe: 'We ran over and had to cut the small-sided game at the end.' Reflect: 'We ran over because I never timed the drills, and I set up the grids while the players waited, so we lost ten minutes. My coaching points on passing weight were actually clear.' Take action: 'Next time I will set the grids up early and time each drill.' This shows the full model: a fair description, honest about good and bad, and a specific action.

Both reflected on the same session. Only Amara moved through all three stages, so only Amara came away with something to do differently.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, a simple reflective model has three stages: describe what happened in the session or task, reflect on why and what you make of it, and take action by deciding what to do differently. You can now describe the three stages, give an example of each, and recognise which stage a reflective statement belongs to. The next lesson looks at what keeps a reflection honest and balanced.

check.body: In the worked example, which part of Amara's reflection is the 'take action' stage?

items.text: Deciding to set the grids up early and time each drill.
Stating that the session ran over and cut the small-sided game.
Explaining that time was lost because the grids were set up while players waited.
Noting that the coaching points on passing weight were clear.

feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Which part says what Amara will do differently next time?
feedback.incorrectFinal: The take action stage is setting the grids up early and timing each drill. Stating what happened is describe, and working out why is reflect.
